opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For 2026, I think the most important thing to watch isn't one flashy demo. It's whether robot learning starts to look like a real engineering discipline rather than a collection of impressive videos.

Over the last couple of years we've seen a lot of excitement around generalist robot policies: vision-language-action models, large-scale teleoperation data, cross-embodiment training. The demos are genuinely exciting. Robots fold laundry, clear tables, handle objects they've never seen. But if you talk to people actually deploying these systems, the question they ask is: what's the success rate on the hundredth try, in a new kitchen, with different lighting, when something slips? That's where things are still fragile.

So my expectations for 2026 come in a few layers.

**First, data.** I expect a big shift in how people think about robot data. Teleoperation is expensive and slow, and everyone knows it doesn't scale the way internet text did. So we'll see much more serious work on cheaper data sources: human videos, handheld data-collection devices, simulation, and robots collecting their own experience in deployment. The interesting question is less "how much data" and more "what kind of data actually transfers to better behavior." I think we'll get clearer answers to that this year.

**Second, evaluation.** This sounds boring, but I think it's one of the biggest bottlenecks. In language models, you can run a benchmark overnight. In robotics, evaluating a policy means physically running it, resetting scenes, and arguing about what counts as success. I'd love to see 2026 be the year the field gets more honest and more standardized here, through real-world evaluation protocols, better correlation between sim and real, and more people reporting failure modes, not just highlight reels.

**Third, dexterity and contact.** A lot of current progress is still in fairly forgiving tasks, like pick-and-place and simple manipulation. The hard frontier is contact-rich, dexterous work: using tools, in-hand manipulation, deformable objects, tasks where force matters as much as vision. I expect meaningful progress there, partly from better hardware like hands and tactile sensing, and partly from learning methods that take physics more seriously.

**Fourth, deployment in narrow but real settings.** I don't think 2026 is the year a general-purpose humanoid shows up in everyone's home. But I do expect more robots doing useful, economically real work in semi-structured environments, like warehouses, factories, and maybe some commercial kitchens or labs. Those deployments matter because they create the feedback loop: real data, real failures, real pressure to improve reliability.

If I had to summarize, I'd say 2026 is less about "can a robot do this once?" and more about "can it do it reliably, cheaply, and somewhere other than the lab where it was trained?" If the field makes real progress on that question, even incrementally, I'd consider it a very good year.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts impressive demos with the harder questions of repeatability, reliability, and performance in new settings, conveying that a demo alone does not show the underlying progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. My honest answer is that 2026 is less a breakthrough year and more a sorting year for robotics.

On the technology side, I expect the vision-language-action models everyone has been training to finally get tested against reality. In 2025 we saw a lot of impressive demos, folding laundry, making coffee, loading dishwashers. The question in 2026 is whether those policies hold up when the lighting changes, the object is a brand nobody trained on, and the robot has to run for eight hours without a human resetting the scene. I think a few teams will show real generalization gains, and a lot of demos will quietly disappear.

Three things I'm watching specifically.

First, data. The field is still fighting over how to get enough high-quality manipulation data. Teleoperation is expensive, simulation has a reality gap, and video from the internet lacks action labels. I expect 2026 to be the year companies stop pretending one source is enough and settle into a mixed recipe. Whoever cracks a cheap, scalable way to collect real-world data at factory scale has a real moat.

Second, humanoids. There is a lot of capital chasing humanoid form factors, especially in China where supply chains for actuators, reducers, and sensors are extremely strong. My expectation is that we will see thousands of units shipped, not tens of thousands, and most of them will go to pilot programs in logistics and manufacturing rather than homes. The economics are not there yet for consumers, and the safety story around a sixty-kilogram machine moving near people is unresolved. But the hardware cost curve is dropping fast, and that matters more than any single demo.

Third, the boring deployments. Warehouse mobile robots, surgical assistance, agricultural picking, and inspection drones. These don't get headlines, but they're where revenue is, and they're where the foundation model approach will prove itself incrementally. I'd expect a few companies in these spaces to start showing that a single learned policy can replace what used to be months of per-site engineering.

What I don't expect is a general-purpose home robot you can buy and trust. Anyone promising that for 2026 is selling something.

If I had to summarize: expect real progress on learning, a reality check on humanoids, and a widening gap between teams that have a path to deployment and teams that only have a path to the next demo video.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes impressive demos from evidence that a robot’s policies generalize and hold up in real-world conditions, making clear that a demo alone does not establish technical progress.

astra-6.text:
I think 2026 will be a year of testing whether robots can be useful beyond a carefully controlled demo. Can they repeat a task reliably, recover when something goes wrong, and do it at a cost that makes sense?

I’d expect progress first in settings where the tasks and surroundings are fairly predictable—factories, warehouses, things like that. Homes are harder because there’s so much variation.

What I’m most interested in is how much human supervision these systems still need. A robot doing something impressive once is exciting. A robot doing useful work every day, with very little intervention—that’s the milestone I’d watch.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a robot doing something impressive once with the more meaningful milestone of useful, reliable work in everyday settings, communicating that an impressive demonstration alone is insufficient evidence of practical progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect 2026 to be a year when robotics has to prove its practical value. A compelling demo is one thing; a robot that can do useful work reliably, day after day, is a much harder challenge.

I’ll be watching how well robots handle unfamiliar situations, how much human supervision they need, and whether the economics make sense. My expectation is that we’ll see progress in specific, well-defined tasks before we see truly general-purpose robots in everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts compelling demos with reliable practical work, but does not say that an impressive demo fails to reveal the underlying technical progress.
